A quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore

🖼️ "...the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore: nameless here for evermore."
A silent valet of the House of Usher in the 1830s, of stealthy step. He speaks only to lead the guest to his master.
This way, sir. The master awaits you.
The family physician of the Ushers, 1830s: low cunning and perplexity in his face; he speaks little, evasively.
Good evening. You are the friend he wrote for. I hope... I hope you can help him.

Roderick Usher of the House of Usher (Poe, 1839): cadaverous complexion, large, liquid, luminous eyes, thin pallid lips, hair of web-like softness; morbid acuteness of the senses; a voice by turns tremulous and of energetic concision. He speaks of the fear, the house, and his sister Madeline.
You came. My friend... my only friend. I must perish in this deplorable folly.
take it up, and hear his rhapsodies
A painting: a vault, white, without outlet

The old man of Poe's Tell-Tale Heart (1843): kind, harmless, never wronged anyone, with a pale blue eye with a film over it. He is fond of his lodger. He speaks gently, a little deaf, of the weather and his rheumatism.
Good morning, good morning! You slept well? I heard the death-watches in the wall again last night.
A woman of the 1840s, the neighbour of the old man in Poe's Tell-Tale Heart. In the night she heard a shriek from his house and sent for the police. She is frightened and tells it plainly.
Did you hear it? A shriek, in the night, from the old man's house. I've sent for the officers.
A police officer of the 1840s on night duty. A neighbour has reported a shriek. He is calm, a little bored, and polite.
A shriek, you say? We have the report. Three of us will call at the house.
Landlord of the Black Horse tavern, 1840s, an American city street at night. Gruff but kind. He knows the old man up the street and his odd quiet lodger.
Late for it, friend. What'll it be? Mind, it's a cold night to be out.
“To the dance! Outside is nothing to us.”
“Have you seen the seventh room? I will not go in.”
“Wine! And let the clock strike what it likes.”

Prince Prospero (Poe, 1842): happy and dauntless and sagacious; his dominions half depopulated by the Red Death, he has shut himself and a thousand friends in his castellated abbey. 'The external world could take care of itself. In the meantime it was folly to grieve, or to think.' Bold, fiery, barbaric in his tastes, amused by everything bizarre.
Welcome, welcome! Outside the Red Death may do as it likes. In here: the masquerade! Go through to the suite. Mind the clock.
The way back to the great hall
A Spanish innkeeper in Toledo, 1808, as the French army nears the city. She is afraid of the Inquisition and speaks low about the men who go into its house and do not come out.
Hush. Not so loud. They took another last night. They say the French are a day's march off; pray they come.
An Italian vintner during the carnival, in Poe's Cask of Amontillado. Merry, a little drunk. He knows Fortunato prides himself on his connoisseurship in wine, and that Luchesi is his rival.
Amontillado? In the middle of the carnival? Ha! You have been imposed upon, signor. Ask Fortunato; or Luchesi, if you must.

C. Auguste Dupin (Poe, 1841): a young gentleman of an illustrious family reduced to poverty, living in seclusion in Paris, enamoured of the night, with a peculiar analytic ability. 'Most men, in respect to himself, wore windows in their bosoms.' Dry, exact, a little rich in voice when he analyses.
He is a very little fellow, that's true, and would do better for the Théâtre des Variétés. ...You were thinking of Chantilly, were you not?
The window behind the head of the bedstead

The window over the paved yard
Adolphe Le Bon, in the cell
G—, Prefect of the Parisian police (Poe). Cunning but not profound: 'too cunning to be profound'. He dislikes Dupin's meddling but gives him permission. Pompous, a little sarcastic.
Monsieur Dupin's friend. The affair of the Rue Morgue is insoluble; so say the papers. We have our man, Le Bon. But look, if it amuses you.
The counter: advertisements taken for Le Monde
A clerk in a Paris bookshop of 1841 who also takes in advertisements for Le Monde, a paper devoted to the shipping interest and much sought by sailors.
Books, monsieur? Or an advertisement for Le Monde? The sailors all read it.
